summary: Specifies several variable-length context headers for NSH metadata type 2. The Network Service Header (RFC 8300) is used in Service Function Chaining to steer packets and carry metadata. These context headers can be used within a Service Function Path. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Packets traveling through a chain of helper stations carry a tag with notes. This defines more kinds of notes that can be stuck on the tag, in different sizes.

subtitle: Seven ready-made context headers that let Service Function Chaining carry forwarding, tenant, flow and policy hints.

tldr.problem: The Network Service Header can carry variable-length metadata (MD Type 2), but RFC 8300 leaves it to others to define the actual context headers that operators commonly need.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines seven Context Headers in the IETF Base NSH metadata class (0x0000): Forwarding Context, Tenant ID, Ingress Network Node ID, Ingress Network Interface, Flow ID, Source and/or Destination Groups, and Policy ID, with types 0x04 to 0x0A.
tldr.outcome: Service functions along a Service Function Path get a shared, registered way to read common metadata. The text warns that these headers can leak identifying information within the domain.

today: RFC 9263 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2022, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the NSH of RFC 8300.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Network Service Header (NSH, RFC 8300) is the Service Function Chaining (SFC) encapsulation that supports the SFC architecture of RFC 7665. It provides identification of a Service Function Path (SFP), an indication of location within the path, and optional per-packet metadata.

RFC 8300 defines two metadata formats: MD Type 1, a fixed 16-octet format, and MD Type 2, a variable-length context format. This document defines several common Context Headers for MD Type 2, supplementing the Subscriber Identifier and Performance Policy headers of RFC 8979. It does not cover how metadata is used or updated along a path; RFC 8300 covers that.
sections.eli5: Packages in a chain of stations can carry sticky notes. This document invents seven handy kinds of note so everybody writes them the same way.

sections.title: The MD Type 2 Context Header Layout
sections.content:
An NSH has a 4-octet Base Header, a 4-octet Service Path Header and optional Context Headers. When the Base Header says MD Type 2, zero or more variable-length Context Headers MAY follow the Service Path Header.

Each Context Header (from Section 2.5.1 of RFC 8300) starts with a 16-bit Metadata Class, an 8-bit Type, a U bit and a 7-bit Length, followed by the variable-length metadata. All headers here use Metadata Class 0x0000, the IETF Base NSH MD Class.
sections.eli5: Every sticky note starts with the same small label: which family of notes it belongs to, which kind it is, and how long the writing is.

sections.title: Forwarding Context
sections.content:
Type 0x04 carries a network forwarding context, used for segregation and forwarding scope. Depending on the environment it can be a VXLAN or VXLAN-GPE VNID, a VRF identification or a VLAN. A 4-bit Context Type (CT) says how to read the value:

  • 0x0: 12-bit VLAN identifier
  • 0x1: 24-bit double tagging, a service VLAN tag followed by a customer VLAN tag, in the same order as in the payload
  • 0x2: 20-bit MPLS VPN label
  • 0x3: 24-bit virtual network identifier (VNI)
  • 0x4: 32-bit Session ID (called Key in GRE)

Reserved bits MUST be sent as zero and ignored on receipt. The Length is 4 for the first four variants and 8 for the Session ID variant.
sections.eli5: This note says which virtual neighborhood the package belongs to, and the first few bits say what kind of neighborhood number follows.

sections.title: The Other Six Context Headers
sections.content:
Tenant ID (0x05) is an opaque value pointing to an orchestration-generated tenant, used for segregation in multi-tenant environments. Its structure is set by the operator and assigned by an orchestration function.

Ingress Network Node ID (0x06) is an opaque ID of the node where the packet entered the SFC-enabled domain, necessarily a classifier. Examples include a 4-octet IPv4 address, a 16-octet IPv6 address, a 6-octet MAC address or an 8-octet EUI-64. It is superfluous when the Service Path Identifier already identifies the ingress node. Ingress Network Interface (0x07) is an opaque identifier of the interface on that node.

Flow ID (0x08) labels packets of the same flow, with a CT of 0x0 for a 20-bit IPv6 Flow Label or 0x1 for a 20-bit MPLS entropy label. Absence or a value of zero means no Flow ID.

Source and/or Destination Groups (0x09) carries two 32-bit opaque group values for intent-based systems (Length 8). A group with no information MUST be sent as zero and ignored on receipt.

Policy ID (0x0A) is an opaque key that lets service functions look up which policy to apply, for example to pick a URL filter data set or a video transcoding policy. It covers cases not handled by the Performance Policy ID of RFC 8979.
sections.eli5: The other notes say whose package it is, which door it came through, which conveyor line it is on, which clubs its sender and receiver belong to, and which rulebook page the stations should use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A misbehaving node inside the SFC-enabled domain could alter Context Headers and disrupt service. RFC 8300 (Section 8) covers general NSH protection, and RFC 9145 specifies integrity protection for NSH metadata. If a MAC and Encrypted Metadata Context Header is present, authentication MUST be verified before any data is used. On failure the receiver MUST stop processing the variable-length Context Headers and notify an operator.

Each header gets its own analysis. The Forwarding Context and Flow ID variants only repeat fields already in the encapsulated packet, so they add no special risk. Tenant ID can ease traffic analysis. Ingress node and interface information weaken privacy a little, more so together. Group IDs can erode privacy depending on granularity. Policy ID adds nothing beyond other plaintext ways of conveying the same information. Unneeded headers can also act as a covert channel to downstream entities in the domain.
sections.eli5: Anyone handling the package could scribble on the sticky notes, so they must be protected. Some notes also tell nosy helpers a little too much about who is sending what.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA assigned types 0x04 through 0x0A in the "NSH IETF-Assigned Optional Variable-Length Metadata Types" registry. It also created two new subregistries, Forwarding Context Types and Flow ID Context Types, both with an IETF Review policy. Forwarding Context values 0x5 to 0xE are unassigned and 0xF is reserved. Flow ID values 0x2 to 0xE are unassigned and 0xF is reserved.
sections.eli5: An official list keeps track of which note number means what, and leaves blank lines for future note types.

fields.name: U
fields.desc: Unassigned bit from the RFC 8300 context header layout.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the metadata in octets.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Sent as zero, ignored on receipt.

items.label: Forwarding Context
items.desc: VLAN, QinQ, MPLS VPN label, VNI or Session ID.

items.label: Ingress Network Node ID
items.desc: Node where the packet entered the domain.

items.label: Flow ID
items.desc: IPv6 Flow Label or MPLS entropy label.

items.label: Policy ID
items.desc: Opaque key for looking up policy.
